content: HIV testing services (HTS) were specifically provided at individuals' homes or other private locations, accompanied by tailored information and services, including contraceptive options. Monthly meetings were conducted with peer educators and healthcare providers to address challenges and plan future outreach activities. By February 2015, over 1,000 male and female sex workers had accessed HTS through the efforts of the Reproductive Health Uganda (RHU) initiative. An unexpected outcome of these community outreach efforts was an increased uptake of sexual and reproductive health services and HTS among men who have sex with men (MSM). Through both clinic-based and community-based activities, 350 individuals were newly diagnosed as HIV-positive, including 73 MSM. Of these, all but 24 individuals, who were lost to follow-up, were successfully linked to HIV treatment and care services. The project demonstrated that local engagement can enhance coordination and effectiveness in programs targeting key populations. Partnerships between stakeholders, peer educators, key population communities, and sensitized healthcare providers helped overcome barriers to accessibility. In Ghana, deep-rooted social stigma against MSM significantly impacts their ability to access HIV-related information and services. To address this, the SHARPER project engaged known MSM community liaison officers (CLOs) to connect with other MSM through social media campaigns. These efforts identified six underground establishments of male sex workers (MSWs) and one telephone-based escort service involving MSWs and their clients. The owners of these establishments agreed to collaborate with CLOs and the SHARPER project to implement mobile HTS services for MSM in Accra. Between December 2012 and March 2014, seven venue-based mobile HTS sessions were conducted with MSWs. Participants were invited by establishment owners, and HTS sessions were provided by SHARPER project staff, CLOs, and selected healthcare providers from the Ghana Health Service. All service providers were trained in rapid HIV testing and sensitized to the needs of key populations. A total of 276 participants attended at least one HTS session, with 56% (n=155) accepting HIV testing. Among those tested, 25 individuals were diagnosed as HIV-positive and were subsequently enrolled in treatment and care services. In Ghana, severe stigma experienced by the MSM community necessitated building trust and fostering collaboration between stakeholders and key population members, which was integral to the program's success. In Namibia, the Strengthening HIV Prevention, Care, and Treatment among Key Populations project began in 2011 with the goal of reducing HIV transmission among MSM, sex workers, and their clients. The project aimed to improve access to HIV prevention, care, and treatment interventions, enhance capacity within local key population-led organizations to provide HTS, and create an enabling environment for advocacy, networking, and collaboration with the Namibian government and stakeholders. Key population-led organizations offered HTS as part of a broader package of sexual health services through standalone, mobile, and moonlight facilities to increase uptake. Trained lay providers conducted group sessions, sexual risk reduction counseling, and HTS. Clients diagnosed as HIV-positive were linked to referral networks for antiretroviral therapy (ART) and other care and support services. Between October 2013 and September 2014, 12,609 sex workers and 2,219 MSM received HIV prevention interventions. A total of 1,959 rapid HIV tests were performed, with 236 clients (12%) diagnosed as HIV-positive and initiated on ART. Additional services included STI treatment, vaccination against viral hepatitis, and Pap smears. In South Africa, the Voices of Change program, initiated in 2011 by Re-Action., focused on sex workers and their clients. The program partnered with the Department of Health at various levels to create an enabling environment for clinical and behavioral prevention services. Four rotating mobile vans provided clinical services in high HIV transmission areas, such as brothels and taverns, on a 28-day cycle. HTS served as the entry point to other health services, including sexual and reproductive health, and chronic illness screening and treatment. Services were provided free of charge, confidentially, and without stigma or discrimination. From 2011 to 2015, Re-Action. conducted 12,993 HIV tests among sex workers at five sites, with a positivity rate of 13%. A total of 1,685 sex workers were newly diagnosed as HIV-positive, and all newly diagnosed clients at one site were registered into HIV care. The program also recruited 14 peer educators from the sex worker population to enhance service delivery. In Bolivia, the HIV epidemic predominantly affects MSM and transgender individuals. The Association Ibis-Hivos developed a mobile health service strategy to provide HTS in convenient and acceptable locations. Services included risk-reduction strategies, condom promotion, syphilis testing, and timely referral for confirmatory HIV testing. Trained peer promoters were integral to the outreach strategy. The mobile unit operated six days a week during night shifts, with two teams providing outreach and rapid HIV testing. Over two years, 6,541 rapid tests were conducted, with 1,116 MSM or transgender individuals, 1,762 female sex workers, and 493 homeless individuals tested for HIV. A total of 117 individuals were referred for confirmatory testing, with 51 confirmed as HIV-positive. In New York City, a program targeting the Garifuna community, an insular ethnic minority of African Caribbean descent, aimed to provide rapid HTS by involving traditional healers as stakeholders and points of care. Pending approval, the program was set to begin in March 2015, funded by the Albert Einstein College of Medicine. Five traditional healers were trained to offer health education and rapid HTS. A preliminary feasibility study demonstrated the potential of this approach, with one healer testing 20 individuals for HIV, three of whom had reactive results. Two were confirmed as HIV-positive and linked to care, while one refused further medical intervention. In Brazil, the Ministry of Health launched the Viva Melhor Sabendo project in 2014 to increase HIV testing among key populations, including MSM, people who inject drugs, transgender individuals, and sex workers. Peer educators provided oral-fluid-based rapid HIV testing in venues frequented by their peers, such as bars and clubs. A computerized system tracked field visits, test results, and referrals. The program, implemented in 35 cities in partnership with 50 NGOs, increased coverage among key populations and reduced barriers associated with clinical health services. From May 2014 to March 2015, 28,400 tests were performed, with a significant proportion of individuals diagnosed as HIV-positive successfully linked to care.
